canonicalExplanation.summary: C++ has C's `for`, `while` and `do`, plus the **range-for**: `for (x : container)`. How you declare x matters. `for (auto x : v)` makes a **copy** of each element: edits change the copy, and big elements are copied every time. `for (auto& x : v)` is a **reference**: edits change the container. `for (const auto& x : v)` reads without copying and without allowing edits, which is the usual choice for reading. Range-for uses the container's iterators, so **don't add or remove elements** during the loop: that can **invalidate** them.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner uppercases every name with `for (auto name : names) name[0] = std::toupper(name[0]);` and nothing changes. Their print loop over 100,000 long strings is also strangely slow. A const auto& range-for reads each large string without copying and does not mutate the vector during traversal. In this lesson you'll implement and debug loops over numeric ranges and standard-library sequences.

examples.title: Reading long names without copying
examples.situation: A const auto& range-for reads each large string without copying and does not mutate the vector during traversal.
walkthrough: **A const auto& range-for:** for (const auto& name : names).
**Reads each large string without copying:** 100,000 long strings are printed with no per-element copy.
**Does not mutate the vector during traversal:** const forbids edits, and nothing will be added or removed while looping.
examples.result: The print loop is fast, and the vector is guaranteed unchanged.

examples.title: The removal loop
examples.situation: A learner erases negative numbers inside a range-for over the vector and the program crashes.
walkthrough: erase shifts elements and invalidates iterators.
Use the erase-remove idiom or C++20 std::erase_if(nums, [](int n) { return n < 0; }).
examples.result: Negatives are removed safely in one call.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: auto in a range-for always refers to the original element, so edits through it update the container.
misconceptions.correction: Plain auto deduces a value type, so each x is a copy. Use auto& to modify elements and const auto& to read without copying.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, why didn't names change?

analogy.example: A range-for with `auto` is like **photocopying each page of a book to read it**: slow for a big book, and your notes go on the copies. `auto&` is **writing directly in the book**. `const auto&` is **reading the book under glass**: fast, and no marks possible.
usefulFor: remembering photocopy vs original vs glass
limitations: Books don't rebind; references can't be re-pointed either.
Adding pages mid-read shuffles the binding (invalidation).

steps.explanation: The vector holds three lowercase names before any loop runs.
auto& edits each element inside the vector itself.
A const auto& range-for reads each string without copying and does not mutate the vector.

nearTransfer.prompt: Given a vector<int>, write three loops: double every element (auto&), sum them (const auto& or auto), and print index and value (index loop). Test with an empty vector.

farTransfer.prompt: Write a function that returns a new vector with each word repeated as many times as its length, without modifying the input while iterating. Then remove all words shorter than 3 characters using std::erase_if and test both.

remediation.explanation: For every range-for decide: **copy, modify or just read?** Pick auto, auto& or const auto& to match. And ask: **does this loop change the container's size?** If yes, restructure.

recap.summary: To write correct loops over sequences, use const auto& to read without copying, auto& to modify elements in place, plain auto only when you want copies, index loops when you need positions, and never insert or erase elements while iterating the same container.
